newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk police fire water cannon at Islamist protest.
newsitem.headline: Turk police fire water cannon at Islamist protest.

text.p: Turkish police fired a water cannon in an attempt to break up a crowd of several hundred Islamist protesters gathered outside an Istanbul mosque after Moslem Friday prayers, witnesses said.

About 200 police, armed with riot shields and batons, scuffled with protesters outside the Beyazit Mosque after prayers held amid an escalating row between Islamists and secularists over state education plans.
One policeman lost his helmet and was punched and kicked after getting caught in the middle of the demonstrators.
Police temporarily stopped those trying to leave the mosque before being pushed back by the weight of worshippers inside.
Scuffles broke out between police and protesters near the entrance to the courtyard of the 16th century mosque in the historic heart of Istanbul.
A police armoured car moved into the crowd firing its water cannon to stop the fighting.
Earlier eight headscarfed women were bundled into a police van and driven away after trying to make a statement to reporters.
The Islamists see the government education plans as a threat to the future of religious schools, known as Imam Hatips.
"Imam Hatips cannot be closed," protesters chanted in the square outside the mosque. "This is Turkey, not Israel," others shouted, holding copies of the Koran in the air.
The protesters, surrounded by ranks of riot police, then sat down in the square and prayed before dispersing peacefully.

"Don't give way to those who want to obstruct your religion," said one man leading the prayers. Some of the crowd thrust their fingers into the air in the sign of an outlawed armed Islamic group, the Great Islamic Raiders Front (IBDA-C).
Mosques in other Turkish cities were largely quiet, according to local officials.
Police put on a big show of force in Diyarbakir, administrative centre of Turkey's troubled southeast, but there were no reports of incidents. The capital Ankara was also quiet.
Under the secularist plans state education would be lengthened to eight years from five, effectively bringing an end to the first section of religious schools.

A parliamentary commission has been debating the draft law this week, but it has been held up by stiff opposition from the powerful Islam-based Welfare Party. The bill is expected to come before parliament's general assembly next week.
Last week 11 people were injured in a protest against the school reforms by several thousand Islamists in Ankara.
The education reforms were a central element of demands by the secularist military in February aimed at cracking down on an alleged rise in Islamist activity while Welfare was in power.
Turkey's first Islamist leader Necmettin Erbakan resigned as prime minister in June under secularist pressure. His government was replaced by a right-left coalition under Mesut Yilmaz.
